newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. airlifts 2,000 more Rwandan Hutus from Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. airlifts 2,000 more Rwandan Hutus from Zaire.

text.p: A U.N. airlift of Rwandan refugees from Zaire passed the 26,000 mark on Thursday but up to 40,000 south of the northeastern city of Kisangani were missing.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR and other aid agencies are using 10 planes to repatriate Hutu refugees on a complex route involving a train through the jungle and ferry over the Zaire river.
"We flew out more than 2,000 today so we have flown 26,248 out since the airlift began on April 27," said UNHCR spokesman Peter Kessler in Kisangani, which fell to rebel forces in March.
But up to 40,000 refugees are still missing from an original group of about 80,000 that fled camps south of Kisangani when they were attacked in April by rebels and Zairean villagers.
More than 80,000 refugees lived at Kasese and Biaro camps south of Kisangani before the attacks, many in poor health.
Now about 15,000 languish at Biaro awaiting repatriation and another 5,000 could be about 80 km (50 miles) south of Kisangani, leaving between 30,000 and 40,000 unaccounted for, Kessler said.

Aid workers say the Rwandans may have fled west, but on the basis of refugees' testimony fear thousands may have died or been killed as reports the Tutsi-dominated rebels are massacring refugees grow.

On Wednesday, rebels citing "security concerns" prevented Sergio Vieira de Mello, a senior UNHCR official, from reaching any refugees beyond Biaro, minutes after he said he hoped that his talks with rebel authorities would bring greater access.
Aid workers have not been able to travel south of Biaro for weeks.

Rwandan officials dispute UNHCR's figures and say only a total of 50,000 Rwandan refugees remain in Zaire, but UNHCR believes 170,000 refugees are still in the country though most are unaccounted for.

The refugees were among over 300,000 who fled west in October from camps on Zaire's border with Rwanda and Burundi rather than join more than a million other Hutu refugees from Zaire and Tanzania who returned home when Zairean rebels began their offensive.
They originally fled Rwanda in 1994 in fear of reprisals for the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
A Rwandan Hutu refugee lobby group urged the international community on Thursday to put pressure on the rebels to stop blocking a U.N. inquiry of reports of massacres of refugees.
The Rally for the Return of Refugees and Democracy in Rwanda said rebels refused to give a U.N. team the assurances necessary for its investigation because they wanted to hide massacres.
U.N. investigators left Rwanda last Saturday after waiting a week for rebels to give them clearance to start work in eastern Zaire to check reports rebel forces were massacring refugees.
The Zairean rebels deny they are slaughtering Rwandan refugees and says killings are the work of former Rwandan Hutu Interahamwe militiamen who helped lead the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.
